  "text": "By morning Tobias had worn a pale place in the church door with the shoulder of his coat.

The sexton found him there and asked whether someone had died.

Tobias moved aside to let her put the key in. He had held his cap all night. He could not get it straight enough to wear.

They went to Maren's after the boats had left. The sexton carried a loaf wrapped in a cloth, though neither of them had suggested she might be ill.

All eleven posts stood along the path. Tobias counted them without moving his lips.

The door was shut. When the sexton knocked, it opened a little.

Inside, the lamp stood unlit on the sill. There was the chip in its base. There was the rug, with one corner folded under where someone had caught it with a foot.

The sexton set the loaf on the table and went through to the kitchen, calling Maren's name in the voice people used for someone upstairs.

Tobias stayed beside the rug.

From where he stood, the window showed no beach. Only water, though the house was well above the tide. He took one step nearer. The sill hid the place where the sand should have been.

Behind him the sexton opened a cupboard, then closed it.

He bent to straighten the rug. Under the folded corner the boards were dry and pale. He pressed it flat with his palm.

When they left, he pulled the door gently shut.

He waited for the latch before letting go."

  "text": "For three days the sexton asked him to fetch the loaf. On the fourth she stopped asking.

The boats came home with their ordinary catches. Men laid fish on the quay and scraped the scales from their wrists. Tobias helped with a rope when it was thrown to him. Nobody mentioned Maren until there was something else to do immediately afterward.

In November a storm loosened the first post beside her gate.

He brought a spade and tamped the earth around it. Then he tested the others. Eleven, still. The work took less time than he had allowed.

Through the window he could see the loaf on the table. The cloth had fallen open. Beyond it was the kitchen doorway and a strip of wall where a calendar hung, turned to the wrong month.

He went round to the door.

Inside, the house smelled of bread gone bad. He wrapped the loaf without looking underneath it. He turned the calendar, though there were now two pages to turn.

Before leaving he stood beside the lamp.

The beach was there. A length of weed lay along the high-water mark, and a gull worried something between two stones.

He stayed until the gull lifted away.

At home he shook the cloth over the ashes and washed it twice. A small blue stitch in one corner held a place where the hem had come loose.

When he returned it, the sexton opened a drawer.

‘Keep it,’ she said.

That winter he used it to cover his bread. Each morning he folded it along the same creases."

  "text": "In March the blue stitch gave way.

Tobias found a needle in the drawer beneath his spoons. The thread he had was brown. He held the corner near the window and made four stitches, none the same length. Then he covered the loaf.

A family took Maren’s house after Easter. Their cart stood across the lane while a boy carried chairs through the gate. Tobias watched the first post bend beneath the boy’s hand.

‘Lift it a little,’ he said.

The boy lifted the gate instead.

‘That will do.’

For several evenings there was light in the kitchen. Someone took down the calendar. A red pot appeared on the sill, and then another beside it.

Tobias went there once with the spade. The woman who answered had flour on her sleeve. He explained about the post. She came outside and held it straight while he packed stones around its foot.

When they had finished she asked if he would come in.

He looked past her. The table stood against a different wall.

‘Not today,’ he said.

She thanked him and took the spade to knock the earth from its blade before returning it.

On his way home he bought a small loaf. It was still warm, and he carried it uncovered.

At supper he cut two slices, then a third. Crumbs caught in the mended corner of the cloth. He brushed them into his palm and opened the back door.

There was enough light to see the step.

He scattered the crumbs beyond it and stayed a moment, listening to someone calling a child home."
